How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability).

Provenance, kept so that a TRACE Research Object (TRO) declaration of the run can be written later from a stored result (metacheck #404; the helpers are in R/provenance.R). Only when code was run (execute = TRUE): * run_results$started_at, run_results$ended_at: when each run of a script started and ended (ISO 8601, UTC, milliseconds); NA for a script that was not started. A script run again in a later pass has the times of its last run. A TRO uses them for each trov:TransparentResearchPerformance. * run_results$exit_status: the exit status of the process that ran the script (0 = ended normally); NA when the process did not report one (a time limit, or Docker failing to start the container). * artifacts: one row per file, with stage (deposit: as downloaded from the repository, hashed from the downloaded file; before_run: the run folder just before the first script ran, after metacheck’s own changes, such as rewritten paths and unpacked archives; after_run: only the files the scripts made (status new), changed (changed) or removed (removed), as an unchanged file is the one listed before the run), path (relative to the run folder, as valid UTF-8, a byte of another encoding written as <xx>), size (bytes), sha256, mime_type (by extension, NA when unknown), source (the file’s address in the repository, for deposit). The package libraries metacheck installs in the run folder are left out, as are metacheck’s own files there (a script’s runner, and the statistical output it writes in statistical_output/). Files metacheck itself copied or made between passes (see modifications, output_copied, file_placed) show in after_run too. A TRO uses the rows as trov:ResearchArtifacts and each stage as a trov:ArtifactArrangement. * modifications$sha256_before, modifications$sha256_after: the hash of the changed script as downloaded and as it ran; NA when the script is not at the same path in both (a script made from an R Markdown file). * environment: the system that ran the code (trov:TransparentResearchSystem in a TRO): metacheck_version, started_at, ended_at, host (R version, platform, operating system), sandbox, network_isolated (TRUE only when every Docker run had --network none; the process sandbox does not stop the network), internet, timeout_per_script, total_timeout, python_local (the Python run outside Docker and its version), and docker: runs (for each kind of run, r_run, r_install, python_run, python_install, the image and the docker run arguments, such as --network none, --read-only, --cap-drop ALL, no-new-privileges, the process limit and the memory and processor limits) and images (for each image, its ID and digests from docker image inspect, its creation time and the R and Python versions its environment declares).

run_results$checked says what the run of each script shows about the code, in five groups, so that a script that does not reproduce is kept apart from one the check could not test: ran (it ran to the end); code_error (it did not reproduce: it stopped with an error of the code or the deposit, could not be read, or needs a file the deposit does not hold); dependency (a package or program was not available: a package that could not be installed or was not loaded, a program outside R and Python, a system library, or R crashing in a package’s compiled code); time (it did not finish within the time limit for one script, or was not started because the time for all scripts had run out); and not_checkable (it could not be checked automatically: it needs a person, the internet, a key or another setting of the authors’ computer, one platform such as Google Colab, Windows or OpenSAFELY, more memory than the run allows, a file that was not downloaded, a screen, or a program that runs it, or it is a file of a package of the code that Python runs only as a module of that package). It is NA for files run inside another script, files that are not an analysis, files not read, and a Docker failure. summary_table counts each group (repro_ran_n, repro_code_error_n, repro_dependency_n, repro_time_n, repro_not_checkable_n), and the report’s first sentence gives them. The traffic light reflects the static readiness signals by default; a script in code_error that stopped with an error makes it red, as a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure, and a script in one of the other three groups keeps it from being green. Calls that need a screen, which the run does not have (dev.print(), dev.copy2pdf(), dev.copy2eps(), savePlot(), windows(), win.graph(), x11(), quartz(), View()), are replaced before the run by calls that need none, which modifications records as screen_call_replaced. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

We introduce the construct of moralistic evaluation-contrasted with compassionate evaluation-as a bridging concept linking do-gooder derogation (DGD) with frameworks of self-compassion and nonviolent communication. We further provide exploratory evidence that moralistic evaluation increases DGD, thereby reducing persuasiveness relative to compassionate evaluation. In a preregistered within-participants online experiment (N = 458 non-vegan German speakers), participants viewed two short videos of a vegan advocating a plant-based diet, presented in moralistic or compassionate evaluation. Manipulation checks confirmed higher perceived judgment in the moralistic condition. Compassionate framing increased likability (reverse DGD) and persuasiveness (r(rb) = .88 and .74, respectively). In a within-participant mediation model (Montoya & Hayes, 2017), the indirect effect via likability (ab = -0.63, 95% CI [-0.75, -0.52]) accounted for most of the total effect of framing on persuasiveness (c = -0.69); the direct effect was small and not significant (c′ = -0.06, 95% CI [-0.16, 0.03]). Interpreted through the lens of self-compassion and nonviolent communication, these findings provide exploratory support for the proposed bridging construct and invite further study.

1 Introduction

1.1 Do-Gooder Derogation

Global challenges, such as the climate and biodiversity crises (Degroot et al., 2021) represent urgent socio-ecological challenges that require not only technological innovation but also profound transformations in individual behavior, collective practice, and public policy (Halman & Nevitte, 2024; Meadows, 2008). Psychological dynamics of interpretation, evaluation, and communication are central to these transitions (Houghton & Metcalfe, 2010; Houghton & Tuffley, 2015; Lönngren & and van Poeck, 2021).

Here, agents of change, such as those advocating for pro-environmental behavior change, risk being derogated, i.e., being put down by others who feel morally inferior to them (van de Grint et al., 2021), fear disadvantages due to social comparison (Raihani & Power, 2021) or feel threatened by changing behavioral standards (Parks & Stone, 2010). This so-called do-gooder derogation (DGD) serves to maintain a positive moral self-image when feeling morally inferior to perceived do-gooders (Bolderdijk et al., 2018; Minson & Monin, 2012; Parks & Stone, 2010; Pleasant & Barclay, 2018; Tasimi et al., 2015). Research has shown that different communication styles influence do-gooder derogation (Weiper & Vonk, 2021).

We introduce moralistic evaluation (ME) and its counterpart, compassionate evaluation (CE), as key factors underlying DGD. We argue that moralistic (self-)evaluation fosters DGD, whereas compassionate evaluation can alleviate it. Our study offers first exploratory evidence relevant to this proposed relationship.

1.2 Effects and Causes of Do-Gooder Derogation

Do-gooder derogation impedes societal change processes. Do-gooders hide their norm divergence to avoid derogation and rejection of their messages (Bolderdijk et al., 2018; Bolderdijk & Cornelissen, 2021; Brouwer et al., 2022; Greenebaum, 2012; Leary et al., 2007), a dynamic theorized to be central to how moralized minority practices unfold at the societal level (Kurz et al., 2020). This reduces do-gooders' opportunities to convince others of their cause. Additionally, DGD leads to a reduction in observers' likability of the do-gooder (e.g., Bolderdijk et al., 2018). Likability is important for persuasiveness (Smith & De Houwer, 2014), and studies have shown that DGD reduces persuasiveness (De Groeve et al., 2022; Sparkman & Attari, 2020; Weiper & Vonk, 2021).

DGD varies with moral superiority and communication style. When dogooders appear highly morally superior, persuasiveness drops (Sparkman & Attari, 2020). Derogation lessens when do-gooders communicate dynam-ically (acknowledging imperfection) rather than statically (presenting behavior as easy and stable), and when gradual progress is valued (Weiper & Vonk, 2021). DGD is also weaker when messages criticize actions rather than people, when do-gooders are credible yet relatable (Sparkman & Attari, 2020), and, as theorized, when they avoid exclusive identities around a practice (Brouwer et al., 2022; Kurz et al., 2020). When observers do not feel involved in the issue that do-gooders are raising (Bolderdijk et al., 2018), persuasion or derogation naturally do not occur. The described effects do not depend on the do-gooders' communication style alone but also hinge on the style of self-evaluation that observers are habituated to, so that merely observing a do-gooder can trigger moralistic self-evaluation and DGD (Minson & Monin, 2012). These findings point to the role of both internal and external evaluation styles, which is elaborated next.

1.3 Moralistic Evaluation as a Factor

Underlying Do-Gooder Derogation

We propose that the factors discussed in the previous section reduce DGD because they involve compassionate rather than moralistic evaluation. While both expose observers' attitude-behavior inconsistencies (see Lavergne & Pelletier, 2016; Zhuo et al., 2022), compassionate evaluation supports observers responding to their attitude-behavior inconsistencies with compassionate self-evaluation rather than moralistic self-evaluation.

Negative moralistic self-evaluation is unpleasant, since humans need a positive self-image for their sustained well-being (e.g. Andrews et al., 2002). Compassionate evaluation, on the other hand, leads to a more positive selfevaluation, evoking less DGD (which aims to protect a positive self-image) (see Figure 1).

Our model treats the term communication style broadly, encompassing both interpersonal communication (how messages are delivered to others) and intrapersonal communication (how individuals evaluate themselves in response). We assume that do-gooder derogation is primarily driven by moralistic self-evaluation, a form of internal communication that can be triggered or amplified by exposure to messages framed in a moralistic tone.

This assumption is consistent with the observation that DGD can be triggered by observation of behavior alone, without any specific communication on the do-gooders' part (Bolderdijk et al., 2018; Minson & Monin, 2012). In this sense, external communication modulates an individual's habitual tendencies toward moralistic or compassionate internal communication.

Note that DGD is expected only when observers share the underlying values of a message (Bolderdijk et al., 2018). At the same time, theories such as Nonviolent Communication (NVC; Rosenberg et al., 2011) and Self-Determination Theory (SDT; Deci & Ryan, 1985), which posits autonomy, competence, and relatedness as basic psychological needs, describe needs like care and connection as universally human.

These needs can provide a motivational basis for pro-environmental and animal-welfare values, even if those values are not explicitly held. Therefore, we expect that the absence of related values, and thus of DGD, will be relatively rare. Alt text. Diagram illustrating hypothesized links: moralistic evaluation increases DGD, which, in turn, decreases persuasiveness. Compassionate evaluation has the opposite effect. Arrows indicate the direction of these effects. Notes. Assumed positive correlations or effects are marked with plus (+), negative ones with minus (-). Arrows indicate the direction of proposed effects. Two-pointed arrows indicate assumed correlations. Square blocks are manifest, and round blocks are latent variables.

Our integrated definition of moralistic and compassionate evaluation involves judging others' intentions or behaviors based on how closely they align with one's current needs, assumptions about fulfilling those needs, and expected social norms (see Rosenberg et al., 2011). Based on Neff (2003a, 2003b), Rosenberg (2005), and Rosenberg et al. (2011), it consists of three components (Table 1).

Kindness

Recognizing the universal human needs that have motivated an action. E.g., a vegan do-gooder acknowledges the meat-eater's need for belonging and takes it into account in their interactions.

2 Individualism Viewing actions and feelings as specific to the person or oneself while disregarding the universality of human experience. E.g., a vegan may judge a meateater, believing their behavior is personal rather than part of a larger human experience.

Common Humanity

Recognizing the universality of human experience. E.g., a vegan do-gooder realizes both vegans and meat-eaters are shaped by their upbringing, and that adopting or questioning childhood norms is a universal human experience.

3 Identification Attributing an observed action and the emotional reactions it leads to in the observer to the stable identity of the person whose action is observed. E.g., a vegan might judge a meateater, seeing meat-eating as a key part of their identity and attributing their anger about animal suffering to this identity.

Nonidentification

Seeing others' actions as needsmotivated and impermanent, depending on their situation and assumptions, and not as defining their identity. E.g., a vegan recognizes that a meat-eater is not defined by their diet, which is just a temporary behavior, and that their own emotions are fleeting mental events.

Notes. ME = Moralistic Evaluation, CE = Compassionate Evaluation

These components connect previous results on DGD and its variations in different communication styles. For example, a dynamic communication style (Weiper & Vonk, 2021) relates to the common humanity and nonidentification components because it highlights the do-gooder's development and their being influenced by a common societal condition. Appreciating small steps is connected to non-identification because it emphasizes the impermanent nature of behavior, which is not part of a stable identity. Not constructing exclusive identities (Kurz et al., 2020) and criticizing actions rather than people (Brouwer et al., 2022) are associated with nonidentification. Being credible while remaining relatable (Sparkman & Attari, 2020) aligns with kindness and common humanity.

The ME-CE construct bridges Mindful Self-Compassion (MSC; Neff, 2003a) and Nonviolent Communication (NVC; Rosenberg et al., 2011) to DGD. MSC emphasizes self-kindness, common humanity, and mindfulness-which are mirrored in CE's kindness, common humanity, and nonidentification. NVC's core questions ("What's alive in us?" ; "What can we do to make life more wonderful?") parallel these same elements. We thus view MSC and NVC as two expressions of a single underlying construct, each focused on intra-and interpersonal communication, respectively (See Julia et al., 2024, for a scoping review of compassionate communication).

An example of moralistic evaluation leading to DGD is a vegan do-gooder judging a meat-eating observer, who then judges themselves negatively, feeling shame and dysphoria. The observer then tries to devalue the dogooder to protect themselves.

Communication styles that include moralistic evaluation are theorized to fuel observers' moralistic self-evaluations, which are unpleasant and may provoke DGD as a form of self-protection (see Figure 1). Under this account, DGD serves to protect against the unpleasantness of moralistic selfevaluation (Minson & Monin, 2012; Parks & Stone, 2010; Pleasant & Barclay, 2018; Tasimi et al., 2015). Moralistic self-evaluation is connected to depressive symptoms and shame (Andrews et al., 2002; Kim et al., 2011; Rimes & Watkins, 2005).

On the flip side, Neff et al. (2007) found MSC to be associated with less anxiety when reflecting on one's greatest weakness (r = -.21, p < .05), suggesting less moralistic self-evaluation. Increases in MSC were associated with increases in well-being (ibid.). Han & Kim (2023) analyzed 56 randomized controlled trials and found small to medium effects of MSC-based interventions, reducing depression, anxiety, and stress at the immediate post-test. Neff & Vonk (2009) consistently found that self-compassion is a stronger predictor of stable self-worth than self-esteem, which is more dependent on moral categories and, consequently, moralistic evaluation. Similarly, Thøgersen-Ntoumani et al. (2017) found that self-compassion reduced upward social comparison concerning body image among young women. Wang et al. (2017) found that those with higher self-compassion were less resigned to their shortcomings and faced them without moralistic self-judgment. Similarly, Leary et al. (2007) showed that self-compassion helps recognize one's part in unpleasant situations without being consumed by negative emotions (see also Rosenberg, 2005). The NVC method has been found to increase empathy (Avichail et al., 2024; Epinat-Duclos et al., 2021; Marlow et al., 2012; Nosek et al., 2014) and decrease empathic distress, social stressors, and conflicts (Wacker & Dziobek, 2018). For example, Avichail et al. (2024) investigated the effects of NVC interventions on solidarity-based collective action (SBCA). The study involved 220 Jewish Israeli participants, and it measured SBCA, outgroup empathy, hope, and other factors in both experimental and control conditions. Measurements were taken before the intervention, immediately after the intervention, and six weeks later. The findings revealed a significant increase in empathy (b = 0.50) immediately post-test, as well as significant increases in SBCA (b = 1.49) and hope sentiment (b = 0.38) six weeks after the intervention. In summary, we assume that DGD is connected to moralistic self-evaluation and can be lessened through compassionate, non-moralistic communication. Exploring such communication is key to understanding how it supports climate action negotiations instead of hindering them.

1.4 Introducing the Present Study

We explored the ME/CE framework by varying the evaluative style in a vegan's self-presentation and examining its association with DGD Two directional hypotheses were examined:

H1: The presence of moralistic evaluation is positively associated with DGD.

H2: DGD is negatively associated with persuasiveness.

2 Methods

2.1 Participants

A total of 821 participants (recruited via snowball convenience sampling from the general population) started the online experiment, of which 494 (60.2%) completed it, and 458 (55.7%) also passed the attention check (7.3% of completed answers were excluded due to failing the attention check). One additional response recorded through the Qualtrics surveypreview mode (a test run by the research team) was removed from the exported data before analysis. Of this resulting net sample of N = 458, 322 (70.3%) identified as female, 127 (27.7%) identified as male, three participants (0.7%) identified as diverse, and six (1.3%) chose not to say. The mean age was 35.10 years (SD = 14.73, range = 18-74). The mode highest completed level of education was the general university entrance qualification (33.6%), followed by a master's (26.6%) and a bachelor's (24.7%) degree. Exclusion criteria were a self-reported fully vegan diet, age below 18 years, and no proficiency in the German language. There was no compensation for participation. Informed consent was obtained from all participants.

2.2 Study Design

We conducted an experimental study with a one-factorial (communication style: moralistic vs. compassionate) within-participant design and randomized stimulus presentation. The study included two experimental conditions (moralistic vs. compassionate evaluation) presented in randomized order. No neutral control group was included, as the aim was to examine the relative effects of evaluative framing styles, not their absolute persuasiveness compared to a baseline. See Limitations for further discussion.

Before data collection, hypotheses, research questions, sampling plan, study design, and data analyses were pre-registered on the https://osf.io/b538c/. We report how we determined the sample size, all data exclusions (if any), all manipulations, and all measures in the study (Simmons et al., 2012).

Due to resource constraints, data collection during the first phase included as many participants as possible, totalling 388. The initial power analysis estimated the required sample size to be 458. This sample size was achieved during a second data-collection period (see Appendix C). The results from the initial and full samples were largely consistent, with no substantial differences.

For H1, an a priori power analysis using G* Power (version 3.1.9.6) indicated that 343 participants would be needed to detect a small effect (d = .20) with 95% power using a two-tailed Wilcoxon test for dependent samples (matched pairs), a within-participant design and a statistical significance level of α = .05. For choice of the expected effect size, see the below paragraph (Han & Kim, 2023).

For H2, we conducted an a priori mediation power analysis, estimating a = -0.162, b = 0.322, and c' = 0 using the R Shyni App Monte Carlo Power Analysis for Indirect Effects by (Schoemann et al., 2020), and based on (Minson & Monin, 2012) and (Smith & De Houwer, 2014). The expected effect sizes are based on a meta-analysis of 56 randomized controlled trials examining the effects of self-compassion interventions on depression, anxiety, and stress, which found small to medium effects at the immediate post-test (Han & Kim, 2023). This power analysis yielded N = 458 with 95% power.

2.3 Materials and Measurements

The experimental stimuli were two 45s to 60s videos of one woman explaining her reasons for her vegan diet (we kept gender constant). We presented the stimuli in moralistic and compassionate evaluation conditions (see Appendix A for complete scripts). We used an item measuring moralistic evaluation as a manipulation check (see Appendix B). Subsequently, we measured the dependent variables (DGD and persuasiveness) using two Likert-type 7-point scales: as a DGD measure, we used three items from the Reysen likability scale (Reysen, 2005) (viewing DGD as a reduction in likability). As a persuasiveness measure, we utilized a scale sub-factor (three items) adapted from the persuasiveness scale by Thomas et al. (2019) (see Table 2 and Appendix B). Due to limited resources, we did not have access to an ethics review board. However, we deem the study low in risk, given the non-sensitive topic and questions, and we closely adhered to ethical standards, such as obtaining informed consent, debriefing participants, and making clear that participation is entirely voluntary and can be ceased at any time, without experiencing disadvantages.

2.4 Operationalization

We designed the stimuli in both conditions to include the three components of moralistic and compassionate evaluation (see Table 1). In doing so, we followed MSC and NVC as fundamental constructs in our definition. A complete outline of the stimuli is available in Appendix A.

2.5 Procedure

Due to resource constraints, data collection for this study was conducted alongside another related project. 1 Data were collected for 16 weeks (November to December 2023 and April to June 2024) using Qualtrics (https://www.qualtrics.com/de/). We collected data on Instagram and Facebook via messages through snowball sampling among people we directly contacted and in climate movement WhatsApp, Signal, and Telegram groups. For example, we sent messages with a template to forward to five others.

After obtaining informed consent and screening for eligibility, participants completed the first part of the survey, which is not relevant to this study.

1 Overall, all participants watched six videos, of which two are relevant for this study. The other four videos varied the communication styles (static vs. dynamic, see Weiper & Vonk, 2021) and the gender of the do-gooder presented in the video (female vs. male), resulting in a 2x2 design. The two videos used in this study kept the gender constant (female) and varied the communication style based on the moralistic evaluation vs. compassionate evaluation construct.

Next, they watched two one-minute videos (for the moralistic evaluation and compassionate evaluation conditions). As mentioned above, data collection was conducted alongside an unrelated project. All participants viewed all six videos, including both videos relevant to this study (moralistic and compassionate evaluation). The other four videos were part of the unrelated study. All videos were shown in a randomized order to reduce habituation and order effects. After viewing each video, participants answered the manipulation check and completed the persuasiveness and likability scales. Participants' eating behavior was assessed in the last stage, followed by debriefing. We randomized the order of appearance of the experimental conditions (videos) and scales (see Table 3 for complete procedure details).

2.6 Data Analysis

For deviations from the pre-registration, see Appendix C.

For H1, we compared likability scores between the two experimental conditions using a two-sided signed-rank Wilcoxon test. For H2, we conducted a mediation analysis with moralistic evaluation as the independent variable, DGD as the mediator, and persuasiveness as the dependent variable. We inferred the relevance of effects based on significance (alpha = .05), confidence intervals (95%), and the minimal relevant effect size (r = .30).

Because each participant rated likability and persuasiveness in both conditions, we estimated the mediation model within the path-analytic framework for two-condition within-participant designs (Montoya & Hayes, 2017). Path a is the mean within-person difference in likability (moralistic minus compassionate evaluation) and path c the mean within-person difference in persuasiveness. Paths b and c′ were obtained by regressing the difference in persuasiveness on the difference in likability, controlling for each participant's grand-mean-centered average likability across both conditions; this allows the relation between likability and persuasiveness to differ between conditions. Inference about mediation was based on a percentile bootstrap confidence interval for the indirect effect ab (5,000 resamples of participants) rather than on tests of the individual paths. All coefficients are unstandardized. Exploratory analyses (manipulation check as predictor, a serial model, and scale order) are reported in Appendix E.

3 Results

3.1 Manipulation Check

The two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test on perceived moralistic evaluation revealed that it was significantly greater in the moralistic evaluation condition (M = 3.32, SD = 1.30) than in the compassionate evaluation condition (M = 1.98, SD = 1.04) (p < .001, r(rb) = .97, 95% CI [0.96; 0.98]), indicating the manipulation was effective (Figure 2). Perceived moralistic evaluation (ME) in the compassionate evaluation (0) and moralistic evaluation (1) Conditions. Alt text. Dot-CI plot: perceived moralistic evaluation is significantly higher in the moralistic condition than the compassionate condition. Notes. Participants rated their impression of being moralistically evaluated by the vegan do-gooder in the experimental video stimulus (manipulation check) on a 5-point Likert scale. Dots represent means, and error bars represent 95% confidence intervals.

3.2 Hypothesis 1: Moralistic evaluation, compassionate evaluation, and likability

To test H1, we conducted a signed-rank Wilcoxon test (two-sided), which showed significantly lower likability in the moralistic evaluation condition (M = 3.1, SD = 1.3) than in the compassionate evaluation condition (M = 4.1, SD = 1.3) (p < .001, r(rb) = -.88, 95% CI [-0.91; -0.85]) (see Figure 3). Likability in the compassionate evaluation ("0") and moralistic evaluation ("1") Conditions. Alt text. Dot-CI plot: Likability is significantly higher in the compassionate condition than the moralistic condition. Notes. Participants rated their perceived likability of the vegan in the experimental video stimulus on a 7-point Likert scale. Dots represent means, and error bars represent 95% confidence intervals.

3.3 Hypothesis 2: Mediation analysis

A Wilcoxon test (two-sided) demonstrated a significant negative effect of the presence of moralistic evaluation on persuasiveness (p < .001, r(rb) = -0.74, 95% CI [-0.79; -0.67]) (see Figure 4). Thus, participants reported significantly lower persuasiveness in the moralistic evaluation condition (M = 2.3, SD = 1.4) than in the compassionate evaluation condition (M = 3, SD = 1.7). Persuasiveness in the compassionate evaluation (0) and moralistic evaluation (1) Conditions. Alt text. Dot-CI plot: persuasiveness ratings are significantly higher in the compassionate condition than the moralistic condition Notes. Answers were given on a 7-point Likert scale. Dots represent means, and error bars represent 95% confidence intervals.

We conducted a mediation analysis with the experimental condition (ME versus CE) as the predictor, likability as the mediator, and persuasiveness as the dependent variable, using the two-condition within-participant approach described in Section 2.6 (Montoya & Hayes, 2017; see Figure 5). For significance testing, we applied percentile bootstrapping (5,000 resamples of participants) (Preacher & Hayes, 2004). The manipulation reduced likability (path a: a = -1.06, 95% CI [-1.18, -0.94]). Within participants, a larger decrease in likability was associated with a larger decrease in persuasiveness (path b: b = 0.59, 95% CI [0.51, 0.68], p < .001), which supports H2. The indirect effect of the manipulation on persuasiveness via likability was significant (ab = -0.63, 95% CI [-0.75, -0.52]), as was the total effect (c = -0.69, 95% CI [-0.81, -0.57]). The direct effect was small and not significant (c′ = -0.06, 95% CI [-0.16, 0.03], p = .320). The indirect effect thus accounted for about 91% of the total effect (95% CI [79%, 105%]). In addition, participants' average likability across conditions predicted the difference in persuasiveness (d = -0.14, 95% CI [-0.21, -0.07]), indicating that likability was less strongly related to persuasiveness in the moralistic (slope = 0.58) than in the compassionate evaluation condition (slope = 0.80). This may partly reflect a floor effect: 31% of participants gave the lowest possible persuasiveness rating in the moralistic condition, compared with 19% in the compassionate condition.

4 Discussion

In the context of global climate and biodiversity challenges, effective communication of pro-environmental behaviors and systemic changes -such as plant-based diets -is essential for sustainability transitions. This study tested moralistic evaluation in communication as a predictor of DGD and subsequent effects on persuasiveness. The key findings are 1) that the manipulation, based on moralistic/compassionate evaluation, significantly influenced perceived moral threat, which was measured as manipulation check, 2) that a high level of moralistic evaluation was associated with lower likability compared to a low level of moralistic evaluation, indicating higher DGD, 3) that a higher level of DGD was associated with lower persuasiveness, and 4) that the negative relationship between moralistic evaluation and persuasiveness ran largely through likability (about 90% of the total effect), with no detectable direct effect. These findings stem from a young and female-leaning sample. While these results have limited generalisability due to the non-representative sample, missing data on presentation order, and the risk of hypothesis guessing (see 5. Limitations), they introduce a new framework and provide a first step toward exploring the connections among DGD, moralistic/compassionate evaluation, and self-compassion.

Our findings provisionally support our theoretical model (Fig. 1) and the moralistic/compassionate evaluation construct. To our knowledge, we are among the first to directly link concepts from the research traditions of DGD and pro-environmental behavior change to NVC and MSC. We assumed this connection for theoretical reasons outlined in the introduction and operationalized it using the moralistic/compassionate evaluation construct, which this study aims to explore.

However, we did not measure moralistic or compassionate self-evaluation directly; instead, we used the manipulation check and DGD measures as proxies. Future research can include direct measurements, for example, via the self-compassion scale (Neff, 2003b (Neff, , 2016;; Neff et al., 2021).

Nonetheless, our results show that the construct is relevant as a manipulator of DGD post-exposure. While the results support our model, the strong contrast between conditions may limit the ability to attribute effects to individual components of moralistic/compassionate evaluation. We present the moralistic/compassionate evaluation framework as a theoretical synthesis and exploratory operationalization, to be refined in future research with more granular manipulations. This study's findings align with prior research on DGD across varying communication styles. Specifically, they are consistent with the assumption that moralistic evaluation in communication about pro-environmental behavior amplifies DGD, potentially as a strategy to protect one's moral self-image in response to moralistic self-evaluation. This result is consistent with earlier findings, which indicate that the components incorporated into our definition of moralistic evaluation contribute to this effect (Bolderdijk et al., 2018; Bolderdijk & Cornelissen, 2021; Brouwer et al., 2022; Kurz et al., 2020; Sparkman & Attari, 2020; Weiper & Vonk, 2021). These results corroborate our initial hypotheses that moralistic evaluation is positively associated with DGD (H1) and that DGD is negatively associated with persuasiveness (H2).

Note, however, that we do not claim that the do-gooders' communication style itself is the sole cause of DGD. Instead, we theoretically posit observers' moralistic self-evaluation-a type of internal communication-as a plausible immediate mechanism behind DGD. Our experimental setup was designed to differentially engage moralistic or compassionate self-evaluation through the two framings; whether this intended process occurred was not directly measured in the present study (see 5. Limitations). In this way, the external communication style acts as a cue for internal processes, which are influenced by previous habits. This view aligns with prior findings that self-threat can occur even from passive exposure to moral exemplars (e.g., Minson & Monin, 2012), and highlights communication style as an important, adjustable factor in this process.

Our findings are consistent with previous research on social comparison and willingness to change. The ways groups may disapprove of members who significantly exceed average prosocial behavior (Parks & Stone, 2010; see introduction) can plausibly be interpreted through the lens of moralistic self-evaluation, whereby observers may judge themselves for engaging in less prosocial behavior than the do-gooder or anticipate judgment from others. The finding that compassionate evaluation communication increased likability is consistent with previous findings, such as that self-compassion is a stronger predictor of stable self-worth than self-esteem (Neff & Vonk, 2009) or that self-compassion reduces upward social comparison (Thøgersen-Ntoumani et al., 2017). Consequently, our results are consistent with the interpretation that moralistic evaluation-framing behavior and those who engage in it as either 'good' or 'bad'-rests on a less stable basis of self-worth, which may support defensive DGD and reduce persuasiveness. We note that self-worth was not assessed in the present study. Conversely, compassionate (self-) evaluation may reduce DGD and the moralistic self-evaluation that contributes to it. This reading is consistent with earlier findings that compassionate self-evaluation is associated with greater willingness to confront one's shortcomings and attitude-behavior inconsistencies (Leary et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2017), although we did not measure self-evaluation.

This study advances previous research by providing exploratory evidence that the moral threat posed by an argument may not be essential for effective persuasion, underscoring the importance of intrinsic motivations instead. The finding that the direct effect of moralistic evaluation on persuasiveness was small and not significant is consistent with this view: its confidence interval excludes positive direct effects larger than 0.03 scale points (c′ = -0.06, 95% CI [-0.16, 0.03]), although a non-significant effect cannot establish that no direct effect exists. If moral threat were a crucial factor in persuasion, a positive direct effect of moralistic evaluation on persuasiveness would be expected, even if offset by negative indirect effects through likability and DGD. This adds another perspective to the assumption that some moral threat (understood as moralistic evaluation) is necessary for pro-environmental behavior change (Brouwer et al., 2022; Chen, 2015; Lu, 2024; Steg et al., 2014). For example, while Brouwer et al. (2022) suggest that a moral threat may be essential for prompting change, they also highlight the importance of fostering self-compassion in communication. Our study differentiates between attitude-behavior inconsistencies and the possible responses to them. These responses can manifest as heightened moralistic evaluation leading to DGD (moralistic evaluation) or increased com-passionate evaluation and intrinsically motivated persuasion (compassionate evaluation condition). An alternative analysis using the manipulation check (measuring anticipated moralistic evaluation) as the predictor points in the same direction once within-and between-person variance are separated (Appendix E): participants who perceived more judgment overall reported slightly higher persuasiveness across both videos, but within participants, perceiving more judgment in one video than in the other was associated with lower persuasiveness, over and above likability. The small positive direct effect found when both measurements were pooled thus appears to reflect differences between participants rather than a persuasive benefit of moral threat. In the condition-based model, the communicator's likability statistically accounted for most (about 90%) of the association between moralistic evaluation in communication and persuasiveness, with no detectable direct path. While generalisability may be limited by the experimental format and the non-representative sample, this finding has important theoretical implications, suggesting a shift from focusing on "who's right" (see Lüdeke, 2023 for an example) to emphasizing human connection as a critical component in promoting pro-environmental behavior change.

One theoretical lens for these patterns is Self-Determination Theory (Deci & Ryan, 1985 , 2000), which holds that behavior change is more readily taken up when it is grounded in existing personal needs and supports relatedness, competence, and autonomy. Compassionate framing may support these needs where moralistic framing constrains them; moralistic framing may additionally evoke shame, which has been linked to moralistic selfevaluation (Andrews et al., 2002; Kim et al., 2011; Rimes & Watkins, 2005) and which we posit as an affective basis of DGD (see Figure 1). Related work is compatible with this reading: autonomy-supportive pro-environmental interventions produced greater attitudinal and behavioral spillover than controlling ones (Geiger et al., 2021), and SDT-informed interventions have shown benefits for motivation and health behavior more broadly (Ntoumanis et al., 2021). We offer this as an interpretive framework for future work rather than as a result of the present study. We assessed neither motivational quality nor need satisfaction, and our outcome was self-reported perceived persuasiveness immediately after a one-minute video, not motivation or behavior over time. Whether compassionate evaluation operates through need support is a question for the between-participants designs we recommend below.

In conclusion, communicating a need for change does not necessarily involve inducing moralistic self-judgments. Reactions to attitude-behavior inconsistencies can also be based on compassionate evaluation, which our findings indirectly suggest may be more conducive to behavior change. We propose that this increased acceptance of behavior change occurs when individuals identify with the communicator's human needs (as reflected in the experimental stimulus: "Caring is important to me") and regard their attitude-behavior inconsistencies with kindness, common humanity, and non-identification, although we did not measure Moralistic Self-Evaluation directly.

Thus, our findings suggest a communication style that clearly addresses an attitude-behavior inconsistency without eliciting moralistic self-evaluation. This style represents a third alternative to the two strategies frequently mentioned in previous research, e.g., Greenebaum (2012): one that supports moralistic self-evaluation and DGD, and another that avoids communicating a need for change, for example, by emphasizing taste or health reasons for a vegan diet. Our study provides initial experimental evidence that this compassionate evaluation communication style is associated with lower DGD and higher perceived persuasiveness, providing tentative guidelines for communicators and policymakers.

5 Limitations and future directions

We acknowledge several limitations of this study, making its contribution primarily theoretical, with exploratory evidence supporting our theory and encouraging future research.

First, the sample overrepresented young, educated, female, and climateconscious individuals, limiting generalizability. Internet access requirements excluded some older adults. Conducted in Central Europe (Austria, Germany, Switzerland), the study's results may be influenced by cultural factors. Future research should use more representative, inclusive sampling.

Second, the power analysis showed different results: 343 for the Wilcoxon tests and 458 for the mediation analysis, matching the total sample size. Overpowered Wilcoxon tests might exaggerate results, but large effect sizes reduce the risk of type I error. Future studies could use smaller, varied samples for these tests.

Third, although the video presentation was chosen to improve ecological validity compared to previous studies that mainly used written vignettes to examine DGD, additional confounding effects might have arisen from the actress's nonverbal communication. To reduce confounding, the same actress presented both stimuli.

The fourth limitation concerns demand characteristics inherent in our within-subjects design. Using the same actress in both conditions improved control over the actress's nonverbal cues and appearance effects, isolating communication-style effects while requiring fewer participants. However, this-combined with scripts that varied only in the sentences in which communication style was expressed-increased the salience of the experimental manipulation and the possibility of hypothesis awareness. Although the sample was naïve to psychology, viewing both clips could have prompted conscious comparison and response biases. Two further design constraints compound this concern. First, the presentation order of the two videos was not recorded during data collection, so the contributions of order and contrast effects to the observed differences cannot be quantified or ruled out. The order of the likability and persuasiveness scales, in contrast, was recorded for 431 participants and did not moderate the association between changes in likability and changes in persuasiveness (Appendix E). Second, the manipulation check preceded the outcome measures; prior work suggests that the mere activation of anticipated judgment can itself be sufficient to elicit do-gooder derogation (Minson & Monin, 2012), so this sequence may have amplified subsequent ratings of likability and persuasiveness. Randomization (N = 458) reduces the risk of aggregate sequence effects, but not of contrast effects or hypothesis awareness. While the magnitude of the observed effects (e.g., r(rb) = -.88) makes a complete contrast-effect explanation unlikely, we cannot rule out that demand characteristics contributed to the observed differences. Future studies should adopt a between-subjects design, use more subtle stimulus variations and multiple actors, place the manipulation check after the outcome measures (or collect it in a separate sample), record presentation order to enable post hoc sensitivity analyses, and include a funneled debriefing to assess hypothesis awareness.

A fifth limitation is the absence of a neutral control group without a persuasive message, which prevents conclusions about absolute effects relative to a baseline level of DGD or evaluative style. This limitation is compounded by the lack of validated measures of dispositional moralistic and compassionate self-evaluation, which are necessary to interpret responses to a neutral frame. For example, low derogation could reflect low moralistic pressure or low habituation to it (i.e., high habituation to compassion).

The study, therefore, serves as a proof of concept, providing a basis for developing such measures and testing their effects relative to baseline tendencies.

As the sixth limitation, we did not directly measure moralistic or compassionate self-evaluation; instead, we included it as a theoretical causal factor for DGD. Future studies can use measures such as the Self-Compassion Scale (Neff et al., 2021) to measure compassionate self-evaluation directly.

Seventh, we acknowledge that the direct comparison of two opposing videos does not allow isolation of individual components of moralistic evaluation. Our design serves as an initial proof of concept rather than a component-specific test. Relatedly, each condition was represented by a single video, so that condition and stimulus are confounded; several videos per condition, analyzed with multilevel models, would allow generalization across stimuli and speakers.

While the moralistic evaluation condition intentionally used extreme expressions of moralistic and compassionate evaluation to operationalize the construct, we recognize that such explicit moral framing may not reflect the typical language of real-life vegans, who often seek to avoid judgment (Bolderdijk & Cornelissen, 2021; Greenebaum, 2012). This reflects the study's aim of a conceptual examination of the model and of introducing the construct as a possible underlying factor of DGD. Future studies should test more subtle variations to assess ecological validity.

Future research can expand on our findings of the close connection between moralistic evaluation and DGD. Our study provides a starting point for research on communicating a need for change, with or without posing a moral threat in the sense of moralistic (self-)evaluation. In particular, there is a need for studies investigating whether compassionate evaluation can increase not only persuasiveness but also real-life behavior, especially in the long term. Future research can also measure moralistic and compassionate (self-) evaluation directly, examining its subcomponents. Then, since moralistic evaluation is common in many Western societies (Hameleers et al., 2019; Hinterleitner, 2020), the effects of this ubiquity of moralistic judgment on expectations, communication, interpretation, and sensemaking processes in daily life are a subject for future study. Overall testing of our theoretical model, which outlines a possible relationship between moralistic evaluation and DGD (Fig. 1), in terms of other relevant factors and explained variance (overall and between factors), will help determine whether it can serve as a research and practice guideline.

6 Practice Implications

Our results suggest that focusing communication strategies on compassion rather than moral judgment to promote pro-environmental behavior could benefit both acceptance and persuasion. For example, climate advocates, such as activists and vegans, might be more effective if they emphasize kindness rather than moral condemnation. This is supported by findings showing that likability mediates the impact of manipulation on persuasiveness, suggesting that the association between moralistic evaluation and persuasiveness in our data ran largely through likability. Therefore, moral threats may be less effective; encouraging self-compassion alongside an ABI is a promising alternative to be tested in future intervention studies.

Methods such as MSC and NVC, on which our definition of moralistic/compassionate evaluation is primarily based, can provide strategies for effective pro-environmental communication. MSC can enhance self-compassion among do-gooders, enabling them to remain clear-headed and empathetic toward others and to resolve conflicts more effectively (Park et al., 2018; Yarnell & Neff, 2013). Regarding communication style, NVC effectively reduces the likelihood that challenges will escalate into conflicts (Džaferović, 2018; Wacker & Dziobek, 2018), facilitating solutions for climate action. MSC and NVC are widely accessible, with numerous courses offered globally, making them practical resources for do-gooders aiming to improve communication. Updating assumptions about effective persuasion can support pro-environmental behavior change, promote shifts in social norms, and help identify ways to adapt to and move through current crises.

7 Conclusion

This study presents the construct of moralistic/compassionate evaluation as a possible influence on DGD. Moralistic communication can impede persuasion and, consequently, obstruct the critical social change needed to address threats such as the climate crisis. This seems to occur because moralistic evaluation messaging makes it more difficult for observers to receive do-gooder messages without responding defensively. We theoretically assume this is because thinking and communicating in a moralistic, evaluative mode form the basis for moralistic self-evaluation, which in turn prompts defensive DGD. In our study, compassionate evaluation was associated with lower DGD and greater persuasiveness than moralistic evaluation. Our findings suggest that do-gooders may want to shift their strategies away from imposing change through moral threats. Instead, they could adopt communication approaches that support observers' intrinsic motivation and compassionate self-evaluation. Our study provides a proof of concept for achieving this by enabling observers to see themselves in the do-gooders' message (e.g., by appealing to universal human needs and shared humanity), thereby exposing attitude-behavior inconsistencies and supporting observers in responding to them with compassionate evaluation.

Such a communication style can help convey the urgency of climate change while simultaneously facilitating observers' non-defensive reception of the message, thereby promoting social change: change by compassion. 9 Open Science and Ethics 1 Statement 2 This study was pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/b538c/. Treating the two measurements of each partic-387 ipant as independent observations (i.e., stacking both conditions and regressing on 388 a condition dummy) yields a = -1.06, b = 0.69, c′ = 0.04, and ab = -0.73, the values 389 reported in the earlier version of this preprint. The within-participant model (Sec-390 tion 3.3) yields identical estimates for a and c, but a smaller b (0.59) and indirect 391 effect (-0.63). The difference arises because the pooled b combines the within-392 person association (a participant who likes the speaker more in one video also finds 393 that video more persuasive) with the between-person association (participants 394 who like the speaker more overall also find both videos more persuasive; slope of 395 person means = 0.73). Only the former corresponds to the hypothesized mecha-396 nism. All analyses in this appendix use unstandardized coefficients and percentile 397 bootstrap confidence intervals (5,000 resamples of participants) unless stated oth-398 erwise. 399 Manipulation check as predictor. We examined whether the results remained con-400 sistent when the manipulation check, measuring perceived moralistic evaluation, 401 was used as the predictor instead of the experimental condition. When both meas-402 urements are pooled, the direct effect of the manipulation check on persuasiveness 403 is small and positive (b = 0.10), replicating the earlier version of this analysis (path 404 a = -0.57, path b = 0.74). Because the manipulation check was measured in both 405 conditions, we then separated each participant's mean across conditions (between-406 person component) from the deviation from this mean (within-person compo-407 nent) for both the manipulation check and likability, and regressed persuasiveness 408 on all four components (standard errors clustered by participant). The within-per-409 son effect of the manipulation check on persuasiveness was negative (b = -0.13, 410 95% CI [-0.21, -0.05], p = .002), whereas the between-person effect was positive 411 (b = 0.18, 95% CI [0.06, 0.30], p = .002). The within-person association between 412 likability and persuasiveness was b = 0.50 (95% CI [0.38, 0.61]), the between-per-413 son association b = 0.78 (95% CI [0.68, 0.88]). The manipulation check was asso-414 ciated with lower likability both within (b = -0.72, 95% CI [-0.78, -0.66]) and 415 between participants (b = -0.41, 95% CI [-0.53, -0.29]). Thus, within partici-416 pants, perceiving more judgment in a video was associated with lower persuasive-417 ness over and above likability; the positive direct effect in the pooled analysis re-418 flects differences between participants.
